chapters.relation: Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.

chapters.file: ch04 - There Is No God in Desperation.md
chapters.relation: Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.

Kellye Byal reads Carrie White through Beauvoir's The Second Sex, treating Carrie's first menstruation, her mother Margaret's ascetic 'Mystic' piety, and Miss Collins/Sue Snell's push toward makeup and the prom as two imposed versions of 'feminine destiny.' Carrie is caught between rejecting femininity (becoming an outcast/monster) and assuming it (surrendering her subjectivity to immanence and the male gaze), so her telekinesis becomes an externalized act of authentic, radically free agency against both scripts. Byal argues her tragic death indicts a failed community of women who never posit themselves as Subjects, illustrating Beauvoir's claim that female subjectivity needs a solidarity of others in which to thrive.

Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.

Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.

Matthew Butkus reads Roland Deschain of The Dark Tower as a parallel to Rama of the Ramayana and Arjuna of the Bhagavad Gita, mapping his cyclical existence onto the Hindu concepts of karma (his coupling with the demon spawning Mordred, letting Jake fall), dharma (the gunslinger's duty to protect the Beams as an avatar restoring cosmic order), samskara (character shaped by all past lives) and samsara (the death-rebirth cycle the Horn of Eld may or may not break). Like Krishna instructing the reluctant Arjuna, the text tells Roland he must 'stand and be true' regardless of misgivings; Butkus concludes the moral for readers is not violence but fulfilling one's own svadharma—to stand and be true in one's own station.

Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.

chapters.file: ch10 - Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship.md
chapters.relation: Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence. Manninen then presses Aristotle: his strict 'only good men' criterion and his debt-bound, property-like view of the parent-child bond fail the flawed-but-loyal Andy/Red and the abusive fathers in The Body, showing human friendship is more complex than his taxonomy allows.

chapters.file: ch11 - Propaganda and Pedagogy for Apt Pupils.md
chapters.relation: Potter and Cobb read Apt Pupil—the blackmail-driven 'teaching' relationship between the boy Todd Bowden and the fugitive Nazi Kurt Dussander—to argue that all effective teaching is propaganda: persuasion by nonrational means (ethos and pathos beyond logos). They analyze the shifting teacher-student dynamic through Foucault's Power/Knowledge, showing power as a fluid relational 'order' rather than a possession, with Russell's definition of power and Nietzsche's Genealogy on the pleasures of subordination explaining Dussander's relief in obeying. Citing Bernays and Chomsky, they contend Todd and Dussander's oppressive, sadism-soaked curriculum merely strips the artifice from ordinary schooling, which has always been a system of control—culminating in Todd's transformation into a killer.

chapters.file: ch12 - The Shining ’s Overlook Hotel as Heterotopia.md
chapters.relation: Elizabeth Hornbeck analyzes King's Overlook Hotel through Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' arguing the hotel is a heterotopia—a socially produced space of crisis and deviance that juxtaposes and inverts normal relations, accumulating time as a 'chronic heterotopia' stuffed with its own ghosts and murders (Mrs. Massey, the Gradys, the 1921 photo). Cut off in winter, it strips away the norms of 'home' so Jack Torrance's inherited monsters (alcoholism, his father's abuse) can turn him from protector into a family-killer. She contrasts the maze-like Overlook with the panopticon of Grand Hotel and Bentham's surveillance-prison from Discipline and Punish, noting that King, unlike Foucault, treats transgression as horrific: the conservative horror genre restores the status quo only when Jack dies and the hotel burns.

holes.name: Transhumanism vs Bioconservatism
holes.what: The debate over whether we should use biotechnology to enhance human capacities and defeat aging/death, opposed by bioconservatives who hold our limits are constitutive of our humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 6 is structured entirely around transhumanism (Bostrom, More) versus bioconservatism (Kass, McKibben, Fukuyama), and the taxonomy has no concept naming either the movement or the enhancement debate.

holes.name: Samsara (the cycle of death and rebirth)
holes.what: The Hindu cycle of death and rebirth from which a soul seeks liberation by working off accumulated karma across lives.
holes.why: Chapter 8 makes Roland's endlessly repeating quest an explicit figure for Hindu samsara alongside dharma, karma and samskara, but the taxonomy's only rebirth concept is buddhist-karma and has no Hindu samsara/samskara slug.
